{ "item": { "id": "10efef82-7491-4d32-9b3f-6b0151fce90c", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Connecting a data source", "short_description": "Choose the right connector type and authentication method for a new data source.", "body": "

Connecting a data source

This guide covers choosing and configuring a source connector — the first step of any new pipeline.

Choosing a connector type

You haveUse
A relational database you can grant replication access toPostgres
Files landing in object storageAmazon S3
An existing event streamKafka
A third party that can push to a URL you controlWebhook

Authenticating

Each connector type has its own credential shape — see the Connectors endpoint for the full parameter list per type.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Least-privilege credentials|body_html=

Grant the connector only the access it needs — read-only replication for Postgres sources, a scoped IAM role for S3, never a superuser or admin credential.

}}

Verifying the connection

A newly created connector reports health: degraded until its first successful read or write, then flips to healthy. If it goes straight to down, double check credentials before opening a support ticket.

Next steps

With a source connected, follow Building your first pipeline to wire it into a full pipeline.

{{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/2df76640-838b-4256-956e-d8a19a602241}}|prev_label=Building your first pipeline|next_href={{cms:item/4201d41e-17fb-495f-976c-9d0c76cacbd9}}|next_label=Transforming events in flight}}", "version_token": "c1f3f7f6-8e3a-4cd5-b25e-b6649db27170", "created_at": "2026-08-21T17:00:07.880Z", "updated_at": "2026-08-21T17:00:25.698Z", "placement_id": "65da7cd3-3805-439a-ab83-5342997746aa", "folder_id": "c3e0ba4a-a491-4265-9848-556d298e6b6b", "file_name": "connecting-a-data-source" } }

{ "item": { "id": "6cb11c67-ca08-4c36-8e37-1bb61973f94e", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Error handling & recovery", "short_description": "How Godzilla retries failed events, when they're dead-lettered, and how to replay them.", "body": "

Error handling & recovery

Every event that fails a transform or a destination write is retried automatically. This guide covers how that works and what to do when retries run out.

Automatic retries

Failed events retry with exponential backoff — 1s, 2s, 4s, up to a per-pipeline configurable ceiling. Most transient failures (a destination hiccup, a rate-limited third party) resolve within the first few attempts.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-retry-config.json|language=json|code={\\n \\\"retry_policy\\\": {\\n \\\"max_attempts\\\": 5,\\n \\\"backoff\\\": \\\"exponential\\\",\\n \\\"initial_delay_ms\\\": 1000\\n }\\n}}}

Dead-lettering

An event that exhausts its retries is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped silently.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=danger|title=Dead-lettered events don't retry themselves|body_html=

Once in the dead-letter queue, an event stays there until you replay it or explicitly discard it — it will not retry again on its own.

}}

Replaying events

Use the Events endpoint's replay action to re-run a specific dead-lettered event once the underlying issue is fixed.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=replay.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/events/evt_8f2c1a90/replay \\\\\\n -H \\\"Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY\\\"}}

Watching for failures

Subscribe to pipeline.failed via Webhooks so you find out about dead-lettered events before a customer does. See also Monitoring & alerts.

{{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/4201d41e-17fb-495f-976c-9d0c76cacbd9}}|prev_label=Transforming events in flight|next_href={{cms:item/dc9f1302-e173-4034-9581-d06efea7d090}}|next_label=Scheduling & triggers}}", "version_token": "fcaf2c64-851f-4ee8-b81e-f41ee07f5647", "created_at": "2026-08-21T17:12:44.325Z", "updated_at": "2026-08-21T17:12:49.578Z", "placement_id": "0b6c15be-6394-4b2e-80ca-660125cbee7b", "folder_id": "c3e0ba4a-a491-4265-9848-556d298e6b6b", "file_name": "handling-errors-and-retries" } }

{ "item": { "id": "4201d41e-17fb-495f-976c-9d0c76cacbd9", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Transforming events in flight", "short_description": "Reshape, filter, and enrich events as they pass through a pipeline using transformations.", "body": "

Transforming events in flight

Once you've connected a source and destination, you can shape the data flowing between them. This guide covers the three core transformation patterns: reshaping events to match your target schema, filtering to exclude unwanted data, and enriching to add context from external sources.

Reshaping events

The simplest transformation extracts and reorganizes fields from incoming events. Use a reshape step to:

  • Map source fields to destination column names
  • Type-cast values (string to integer, object to JSON)
  • Flatten nested objects or arrays
  • Rename fields that conflict with reserved words

Each reshape rule is a source_path → destination_field mapping. Unmapped fields are dropped by default.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline.config.json|language=json|code={"transforms": [{"type": "reshape", "mappings": {"user.id": "user_id", "user.email": "email", "event_time": "created_at"}}]}}}

Filtering events

Not every event should reach your destination. Use filters to keep only the events you care about:

  • Exclude test or debug events before they pollute production data
  • Route events based on type or country to different destinations
  • Drop events that fail validation or have missing required fields

Filters use simple boolean expressions: field == value, field > 100, or field IN (a, b, c).

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline.config.json|language=json|code={"transforms": [{"type": "filter", "condition": "environment != 'test' AND user_id IS NOT NULL"}]}}} {{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Filter early|body_html=

Place filter steps near the beginning of your pipeline to avoid wasted processing on events you'll discard.

}}

Enriching events

Enrich events by joining them with reference data from an external source — typically a database lookup or API call:

  • Look up a customer's plan tier by user_id to route them to the right analytics table
  • Fetch geolocation data from an IP address in the event
  • Add a standardized product category to a SKU field

Enrichments are cached to avoid hammering external sources on every event. Failed lookups can be configured to drop the event or pass it through with a null enrichment field.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline.config.json|language=json|code={"transforms": [{"type": "enrich", "source": "postgres_reference", "join_key": "product_id", "lookup_field": "sku", "cache_ttl_seconds": 3600, "fields_to_add": ["category", "vendor"]}]}}}

Chaining transformations

Combine multiple transformations in sequence. The pipeline processes them left to right, so the output of one stage becomes the input to the next:

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline.config.json|language=json|code={"transforms": [{"type": "filter", "condition": "environment != 'test'"}, {"type": "reshape", "mappings": {"user.id": "user_id"}}, {"type": "enrich", "source": "lookups", "join_key": "user_id"}]}}}

Monitoring transformation health

Watch for transformation failures in the pipeline health dashboard:

  • Filter dropout rate — if you're suddenly filtering 90% of events, check your filter condition for regressions

{ "item": { "id": "dc9f1302-e173-4034-9581-d06efea7d090", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Scheduling & triggers", "short_description": "Run a pipeline on a cron schedule or trigger it directly from incoming events.", "body": "

Scheduling & triggers

A pipeline runs either on a schedule or in response to incoming events. This guide covers both.

Scheduled pipelines

Set a schedule (a cron expression) when creating or updating a pipeline via the Pipelines endpoint. Godzilla runs the pipeline once per schedule tick, processing whatever new data is available from the source since the last run.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=schedule.json|language=json|code={ "schedule": "0 */4 * * *" }}}

Event-triggered pipelines

Omit schedule and the pipeline instead runs continuously, processing events as its source connector emits them — the right choice for sources like Kafka or a Webhook connector where near-real-time matters.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Choosing between them|body_html=

Use a schedule for sources that batch naturally (a nightly file drop to S3). Use event-triggered for anything where minutes matter.

}}

Pausing and resuming

A paused pipeline skips scheduled ticks entirely and buffers nothing for event-triggered sources — resuming picks up new events going forward, not a backlog. To reprocess a time range instead, see the replay flow in Handling errors & retries.

{{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/062cc815-2b65-45b1-b36c-6ea67dfd1a0c}}|prev_label=Handling errors & retries|next_href={{cms:item/522ba05b-8a21-43dd-82ac-ece908ce14b4}}|next_label=Monitoring & alerts}}", "version_token": "79959961-9dce-4f2e-b4ca-b957b12122d0", "created_at": "2026-08-20T14:12:47.158Z", "updated_at": "2026-08-20T15:07:12.086Z", "placement_id": "8ed279da-c9eb-46e0-bd2f-4f15df9f1c76", "folder_id": "c3e0ba4a-a491-4265-9848-556d298e6b6b", "file_name": "scheduling-and-triggers" } }

{ "item": { "id": "522ba05b-8a21-43dd-82ac-ece908ce14b4", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Monitoring & alerts", "short_description": "Watch pipeline health and get notified of failures via webhooks before they become incidents.", "body": "

Monitoring & alerts

Keep an eye on a running pipeline without babysitting it manually.

Connector health

Poll a connector's health field via the Connectors endpoint, or better, subscribe to connector.error so you're notified the moment it degrades.

Subscribing to pipeline lifecycle events

The most reliable way to monitor a pipeline is a webhook subscription on pipeline.failed and connector.error.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=subscribe.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/webhooks \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \ -d '{"url":"https://you.example.com/hooks/godzilla","events":["pipeline.failed","connector.error"]}'}} {{ds:component/alert|variant=success|title=Recommended baseline|body_html=

At minimum, subscribe to pipeline.failed for every production pipeline. It's the single highest-signal event for catching problems before customers do.

}}

Dead-letter queue depth

A growing dead-letter queue is an early warning sign, not just a symptom — see Handling errors & retries for how events end up there and how to drain them.

{{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/dc9f1302-e173-4034-9581-d06efea7d090}}|prev_label=Scheduling & triggers|next_href={{cms:item/60d7d27a-ceda-4034-b98e-8b1181ca5c84}}|next_label=Guides}}", "version_token": "352ca016-eadc-40fe-8762-27fd446580a2", "created_at": "2026-08-20T14:12:53.717Z", "updated_at": "2026-08-20T15:07:12.090Z", "placement_id": "1bf22621-3ed5-4c90-b1d8-47770d74ffd7", "folder_id": "c3e0ba4a-a491-4265-9848-556d298e6b6b", "file_name": "monitoring-and-alerts" } }

input.body:
Transforming events in flight

Once you've connected a source and destination, you can shape the data flowing between them. This guide covers the three core transformation patterns: reshaping events to match your target schema, filtering to exclude unwanted data, and enriching to add context from external sources.

{{ds:component/docs-toc|items_html=
  • Reshaping events
  • Filtering events
  • Enriching events
  • Chaining transformations
  • Monitoring transformation health
  • Next steps
    • }}

    Reshaping events

    The simplest transformation extracts and reorganizes fields from incoming events. Use a reshape step to:

    • Map source fields to destination column names
    • Type-cast values (string to integer, object to JSON)
    • Flatten nested objects or arrays
    • Rename fields that conflict with reserved words

    Each reshape rule is a source_path → destination_field mapping. Unmapped fields are dropped by default.

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline.config.json|language=json|code={\"transforms\": [{\"type\": \"reshape\", \"mappings\": {\"user.id\": \"user_id\", \"user.email\": \"email\", \"event_time\": \"created_at\"}}]}}}

    Filtering events

    Not every event should reach your destination. Use filters to keep only the events you care about:

    • Exclude test or debug events before they pollute production data
    • Route events based on type or country to different destinations
    • Drop events that fail validation or have missing required fields

    Filters use simple boolean expressions: field == value, field > 100, or field IN (a, b, c).

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline.config.json|language=json|code={\"transforms\": [{\"type\": \"filter\", \"condition\": \"environment != 'test' AND user_id IS NOT NULL\"}]}}} {{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Filter early|body_html=

    Place filter steps near the beginning of your pipeline to avoid wasted processing on events you'll discard.

    }}

    Enriching events

    Enrich events by joining them with reference data from an external source — typically a database lookup or API call:

    • Look up a customer's plan tier by user_id to route them to the right analytics table
    • Fetch geolocation data from an IP address in the event
    • Add a standardized product category to a SKU field

    Enrichments are cached to avoid hammering external sources on every event. Failed lookups can be configured to drop the event or pass it through with a null enrichment field.

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline.config.json|language=json|code={\"transforms\": [{\"type\": \"enrich\", \"source\": \"postgres_reference\", \"join_key\": \"product_id\", \"lookup_field\": \"sku\", \"cache_ttl_seconds\": 3600, \"fields_to_add\": [\"category\", \"vendor\"]}]}}}

    Chaining transformations

    Combine multiple transformations in sequence. The pipeline processes them left to right, so the output of one stage becomes the input to the next:

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline.config.json|language=json|code={\"transforms\": [{\"type\": \"filter\", \"condition\": \"environment != 'test'\"}, {\"type\": \"reshape\", \"mappings\": {\"user.id\": \"user_id\"}}, {\"type\": \"enrich\", \"source\": \"lookups\", \"join_key\": \"user_id\"}]}}}

    Monitoring transformation health

    Watch for transformation failures in the pipeline health dashboard:

    • Filter dropout rate — if you're suddenly filtering 90% of events, check your filter condition for regressions
    • Reshape field errors — unmapped source fields mean your schema changed; add new mappings or adjust downstream expectations
    • Enrichment failures — if your reference data source goes down, events may be dropped or delayed depending on your fallback policy

    Next steps

    With transformation rules in place, continue to Handling errors & retries to learn how the pipeline deals with transformation failures and malformed data.

    {{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/3448ffab-598c-46e7-bda6-e7cdc4a1e7c6}}|prev_label=Connecting a data source|next_href={{cms:item/062cc815-2b65-45b1-b36c-6ea67dfd1a0c}}|next_label=Handling errors & retries}}

input.body:
Error handling & recovery

Every event that fails a transform or a destination write is retried automatically. This guide covers how that works and what to do when retries run out.

{{ds:component/docs-toc|items_html=
  • Automatic retries
  • Dead-lettering
  • Replaying events
  • Watching for failures
    • }}

    Automatic retries

    Failed events retry with exponential backoff — 1s, 2s, 4s, up to a per-pipeline configurable ceiling. Most transient failures (a destination hiccup, a rate-limited third party) resolve within the first few attempts.

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-retry-config.json|language=json|code={\\n \\\"retry_policy\\\": {\\n \\\"max_attempts\\\": 5,\\n \\\"backoff\\\": \\\"exponential\\\",\\n \\\"initial_delay_ms\\\": 1000\\n }\\n}}}

    Dead-lettering

    An event that exhausts its retries is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped silently.

    {{ds:component/alert|variant=danger|title=Dead-lettered events don't retry themselves|body_html=

    Once in the dead-letter queue, an event stays there until you replay it or explicitly discard it — it will not retry again on its own.

    }}

    Replaying events

    Use the Events endpoint's replay action to re-run a specific dead-lettered event once the underlying issue is fixed.

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=replay.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/events/evt_8f2c1a90/replay \\\\n -H \\\"Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY\\\"}}

    Watching for failures

    Subscribe to pipeline.failed via Webhooks so you find out about dead-lettered events before a customer does. See also Monitoring & alerts.

    {{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/4201d41e-17fb-495f-976c-9d0c76cacbd9}}|prev_label=Transforming events in flight|next_href={{cms:item/dc9f1302-e173-4034-9581-d06efea7d090}}|next_label=Scheduling & triggers}}

input.body:
Building your first pipeline

This guide walks through creating a pipeline end to end: a source connector, a destination connector, and the pipeline that ties them together.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Before you start|body_html=

You'll need an API key. See Authentication in Getting Started if you don't have one yet.

}} {{ds:component/docs-toc|items_html=
  • 1. Create a source connector
  • 2. Create a destination connector
  • 3. Create the pipeline
  • Next steps
    • }}

    1. Create a source connector

    We'll pull orders from Postgres. See Connectors for the full catalog of types.

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-source.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/connectors \\\\\\n -H \"Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY\" \\\\\\n -d '{\"type\":\"postgres\",\"direction\":\"source\",\"config\":{\"connection_string\":\"postgres://...\"}}'}} {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create_source.go|language=go|code=package main\\n\\nimport (\\n\t\"context\"\\n\t\"log\"\\n\t\"os\"\\n\\n\t\"github.com/godzilladev/godzilla-go\"\\n)\\n\\nfunc main() {\\n\tclient := godzilla.NewClient(\\n\t\tgodzilla.WithAPIKey(os.Getenv(\"GODZILLA_API_KEY\")),\\n\t)\\n\\n\tconnector, err := client.Connectors.Create(context.Background(), &godzilla.CreateConnectorRequest{\\n\t\tType: \"postgres\",\\n\t\tDirection: \"source\",\\n\t\tConfig: map[string]interface{}{\\n\t\t\t\"connection_string\": \"postgres://...\",\\n\t\t},\\n\t})\\n\tif err != nil {\\n\t\tlog.Fatalf(\"failed to create connector: %v\", err)\\n\t}\\n\tlog.Printf(\"Created connector: %s\\n\", connector.ID)\\n}}}

    2. Create a destination connector

    We'll write to Snowflake.

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-destination.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/connectors \\\\\\n -H \"Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY\" \\\\\\n -d '{\"type\":\"snowflake\",\"direction\":\"destination\",\"config\":{\"account\":\"...\"}}'}} {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create_destination.go|language=go|code=package main\\n\\nimport (\\n\t\"context\"\\n\t\"log\"\\n\t\"os\"\\n\\n\t\"github.com/godzilladev/godzilla-go\"\\n)\\n\\nfunc main() {\\n\tclient := godzilla.NewClient(\\n\t\tgodzilla.WithAPIKey(os.Getenv(\"GODZILLA_API_KEY\")),\\n\t)\\n\\n\tconnector, err := client.Connectors.Create(context.Background(), &godzilla.CreateConnectorRequest{\\n\t\tType: \"snowflake\",\\n\t\tDirection: \"destination\",\\n\t\tConfig: map[string]interface{}{\\n\t\t\t\"account\": \"...\",\\n\t\t},\\n\t})\\n\tif err != nil {\\n\t\tlog.Fatalf(\"failed to create connector: %v\", err)\\n\t}\\n\tlog.Printf(\"Created connector: %s\\n\", connector.ID)\\n}}}

    3. Create the pipeline

    Full request/response details are in the Pipelines endpoint reference.

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-pipeline.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines \\\\\\n -H \"Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY\" \\\\\\n -d '{\"name\":\"ingest-orders\",\"source_connector_id\":\"conn_pg_orders\",\"destination_connector_id\":\"conn_snowflake_dw\"}'}} {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create_pipeline.go|language=go|code=package main\\n\\nimport (\\n\t\"context\"\\n\t\"log\"\\n\t\"os\"\\n\\n\t\"github.com/godzilladev/godzilla-go\"\\n)\\n\\nfunc main() {\\n\tclient := godzilla.NewClient(\\n\t\tgodzilla.WithAPIKey(os.Getenv(\"GODZILLA_API_KEY\")),\\n\t)\\n\\n\tpipeline, err := client.Pipelines.Create(context.Background(), &godzilla.CreatePipelineRequest{\\n\t\tName: \"ingest-orders\",\\n\t\tSourceConnectorID: \"conn_pg_orders\",\\n\t\tDestinationConnectorID: \"conn_snowflake_dw\",\\n\t})\\n\tif err != nil {\\n\t\tlog.Fatalf(\"failed to create pipeline: %v\", err)\\n\t}\\n\tlog.Printf(\"Created pipeline: %s\\n\", pipeline.ID)\\n}}}

    The pipeline starts in draft state. Activate it once you're ready to start processing events.

    Next steps

    Now that events are flowing, read Handling errors & retries to see what happens when a write fails, or Monitoring & alerts to watch it run.

    {{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/60d7d27a-ceda-4034-b98e-8b1181ca5c84}}|prev_label=Guides|next_href={{cms:item/3448ffab-598c-46e7-bda6-e7cdc4a1e7c6}}|next_label=Connecting a data source}}
